The [payment-history workflow](profile-context-and-a-second-outcome.qmd) combines
account context, repeated transactions, and later outcomes. The
[account model](nested-context-and-account-outcomes.qmd) adds several levels of context and targets.
Once that pattern is familiar, apply it to a retailer's purchase histories and
customer retention decisions.

The review, study-reporting, and market examples later on this page are
optional applications to other event domains. Each keeps attributes at the
root, related records in a branch, and a target describing a later outcome.

## Retail: who will make no purchase next week?

A retail team can rank recently active customers by their estimated chance of
making no purchase next week, then choose whom to contact. Whether that contact
changes purchasing requires a separate intervention evaluation.

Define the population as customers who bought something in the preceding seven
days. For each customer, predict `inactive_next_7_days`: true when there is no
purchase after the decision time through seven days later. This gives the team
a specific measure of short-term inactivity.

Customer attributes describe the person. Their purchase history describes
interactions: which articles they bought, through which channels, and when
they were booked. Your application joins those records and keeps only
information available at the decision time before supplying the observation
to RelFlow.

### One illustrative observation

At the May 28, 2026 decision, a training observation contains customer
attributes and purchases booked by that date. The root Boolean records customer
inactivity during the seven days after that common snapshot cutoff and is
attached once that window has completed:

```yaml
customer_age: 34
club_member_status: ACTIVE
recent_purchases:
  - booked_at: "2026-05-22T10:00:00"
    article_id: article-17
    amount: 32.00
    sales_channel: online
  - booked_at: "2026-05-26T17:30:00"
    article_id: article-03
    amount: 56.20
    sales_channel: store
inactive_next_7_days: true
```

### Describe the customer and their purchases

```python
import relflow as rf

model = rf.Model.sm(
    customer_age=rf.Number,
    club_member_status=rf.Category,
    recent_purchases=rf.Branch(
        length=32,
        overflow="tail",
        booked_at=rf.DateParts(
            dateparts=["day_of_month", "day_of_week", "hour_of_day"],
        ),
        article_id=rf.Category,
        amount=rf.Number,
        sales_channel=rf.Category,
    ),
    inactive_next_7_days=rf.Boolean(mask=True),
)
```

```{typst}
//| label: fig-retail-retention
//| fig-cap: "The customer is the subject: attributes at the root, purchases in a branch, and one hidden outcome for the customer."
//| fig-alt: "A customer root contains customer_age Number, club_member_status Category, a repeated recent_purchases branch with booked_at DateParts, article_id Category, amount Number, and sales_channel Category, and a hidden inactive_next_7_days Boolean target at the root."
#tree(node("customer", kind: "root", children: (

  node("inactive_next_7_days", width: 160pt, kind: "target", type: "Boolean", detail: "One per customer"),
)))
```

The customer is the subject of the prediction; each purchase keeps its own
article, amount, channel, and booking date together. Supply purchases oldest to
newest so the branch retains the most recent 32. Choose that capacity for the
history your application needs. `mask=True` keeps the later outcome out of the
inputs while using it as supervision. This customer target is always masked,
so omit it when requesting a new prediction. Retain customer identifiers and
decision times in your application to associate the result with the right
customer snapshot.

A table containing days since the last purchase, purchase counts, spending
totals, and channel counts is a sensible baseline. Keeping individual purchases
gives the model access to combinations of article, amount, channel, and timing
that those summaries may omit. Compare both approaches on later decision
windows with the same eligible customers and available evidence. Use
relational context when that comparison justifies its preparation and
processing cost.

### Train and predict from Parquet files

Prepare your application's training and validation files with one customer
observation per row and the fields above. Use earlier decision windows for
training and later windows for validation:

```python
data = rf.ArrowDataModule(
    train="retention/train.parquet",
    validate="retention/validation.parquet",
)
model.fit(data, batch_size=128, max_epochs=20)
```

For new decisions, prepare the same customer attributes and purchase history
in a request file, omitting `inactive_next_7_days`:

```python
requests = rf.ArrowDataModule(
    predict="retention/requests.parquet",
)
predictions = model.predict(datamodule=requests, batch_size=256, devices=1)
```

[Read predictions](read-predictions.qmd) explains how to read the
result under `predictions.inactive_next_7_days`. The schema address remains
`/inactive_next_7_days`.

## Engagement: will an active reviewer stop posting?

A team seeking fresh product feedback can use the same structure to anticipate
review inactivity. Choose customers who posted a review in the preceding 91
days, and define the target as no review during the following 91 days.

Customer attributes stay at the root. Earlier reviews form the history, keeping
each product, rating, and review date together. This outcome measures
participation in a feedback channel: a customer can keep buying without posting
a review. Compare a richer review history with review recency and frequency
summaries before using it to prioritize invitations for feedback.

## Clinical studies: which studies will report larger totals?

A trial operations team may want to anticipate which ongoing studies will
report larger totals of affected subjects. For studies that have already
started, define a 365-day outcome: the sum of `subjects_affected` in reports
marked `serious` or `deaths` that arrive after the decision time through
365 days later.

Study attributes provide the root context. Earlier reports form a branch,
keeping report type, affected-subject count, and report date together. The later
total is a masked numeric target. This sum can count a person in more than one
report, so it does not measure unique affected people or an individual's risk.
Define how incomplete reporting affects label availability; a missing report
does not establish a zero total.

## Markets: what will tomorrow's close be?

A market-data application can supply daily bars and ask for the next trading
day's closing price. A bar is a multivariate event: opening, high, low, and
closing prices plus volume belong to the same interval. The history-and-target
pattern stays the same:

```python
market_model = rf.Model.xs(
    daily_bars=rf.Branch(
        length=64,
        overflow="tail",
        booked_at=rf.DateParts(
            dateparts=["day_of_month", "day_of_week", "hour_of_day"],
        ),
        open=rf.Number,
        high=rf.Number,
        low=rf.Number,
        close=rf.Number,
        volume=rf.Number,
    ),
    next_close=rf.Number(mask=True),
)
```

Each bar keeps its price and volume measurements together. Prepare observations
at the end of a trading day, including only completed bars known then.
`booked_at` supplies calendar context for each completed bar. The
`next_close` label comes from the following trading day and becomes available
after that day closes. Train from Parquet files through `ArrowDataModule`, as
above, using files prepared for this market schema.

This defines one future-value prediction. If the application needs several
future steps, define their target structure and evaluation horizon explicitly.
Include a last-known-close baseline when evaluating this forecast.

## Keep the decision time in every example

Every example follows [Prepare observations](prepare-observations.qmd):
construct each observation as it could have been seen at its decision time,
attach labels from the specified future window, and let that window finish
before treating them as observed outcomes. Two points matter more outside
payments. An event that happened earlier but was reported later is unavailable
until its report arrives, and mutable customer or study attributes need the
values known at the decision time.

The same entity can appear at several decision times. Keep later evaluation
windows separate and control overlap between their label periods and training
examples. [Evaluation](evaluation.qmd) explains the comparison;
[Preprocessing](../guides/preprocessing.qmd) covers preparing the nested inputs.

This is the end of the learning path. To understand how the model combines
the evidence, continue with the [model tree](../concepts/model-tree.qmd)
and [how fields interact](../concepts/how-fields-interact.qmd). To
put a model into production, see [Serving](../guides/serving.qmd) and
[Batch inference](../guides/batch-inference.qmd).
